voiceover.text: So, what does national health data really tell us? Here's a puzzle. One person says Australians are among the healthiest people in the world. Another says Australia has a chronic disease crisis. Both are quoting the same national health report, and both can be right. How? And before you pick a side, what would you need to know? Living longer is good news. But healthy for whom, and healthy for how many of those years?

scenes.title: the rule: read the trend, not the number

voiceover.text: First, the syllabus rule for this whole topic. You don't need to know the latest rates. You need to understand the trends, because a rate goes out of date next year, and the skill doesn't. In Year 11, you asked five questions of any table, including which way it's moving. Now open that one up into four. Direction: rising, falling or flat? Shape: steady, speeding up, or stalled? Distribution: the same for everyone, or is a gap opening or closing? And cause: what explains it, and what would you check? A number is evidence for a claim. It isn't the claim.

scenes.title: what we die of, and what we live with

voiceover.text: Year 11 gave you the measures: mortality counts deaths, morbidity counts illness and disability, incidence counts new cases, and prevalence counts everyone living with it. Read them as two lists. In 2025, the leading causes of death were dementia, coronary heart disease, stroke, lung cancer and lung disease. But the leading causes of illness are different: mental health conditions, and muscle and bone conditions like back pain. Plan only from the death list, and you'd underfund what most people actually live with. And here's the first answer to the puzzle. When treatment keeps people alive without curing them, deaths fall, and the number living with the condition rises. That's success, but it means more long-term care.

scenes.title: life expectancy, and what it hides

voiceover.text: Life expectancy is the headline number: how long a baby born now would live on average, if today's death rates never changed. It has risen for over a century. For 2022 to 2024, it was eighty-one point one years for males and eighty-five point one for females, so the population sits in between. The gap is four years, down from about six in the mid-nineties. Three things hide in that number. It's a projection, so it gets revised. It's an average, so a group can be stuck while the total rises. And it counts years, not health. Some of those extra years are lived with illness or disability.
And the sex gap? Biology plays a part, but the gap has shrunk, and biology doesn't change that fast. Risk-taking, dangerous jobs, smoking, drinking and not seeking help explain a gap that moves.

scenes.title: why "they chose to" isn't an analysis

voiceover.text: Now risky health behaviours, like smoking, heavy drinking, inactivity and poor diet. The data shows they aren't spread evenly. They cluster by income, education, job, remoteness and background. Choices alone wouldn't make such regular patterns, so something in people's circumstances is producing them. These are sociological causes. Money, work hours and insecure housing limit what's realistic. Health literacy is uneven. Some areas lack footpaths, fresh food or a nearby clinic, and have more takeaway shops and ads. What's normal among your family and friends spreads. And low control over your life brings stress, and ways of coping with it. The behaviour is the last link in a long chain, not the first.

scenes.title: where the inequities are, and what can be done

voiceover.text: Read any national report by group, and the same rows appear. Outcomes are poorer, and improve more slowly, for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, people on the lowest incomes, people in rural and remote areas, some culturally and linguistically diverse communities, and people with disability. Remember, an inequity isn't just any difference. It's avoidable, unnecessary and unfair, which means it can be fixed. So what can be done? Bring services to people, with outreach, telehealth, interpreters and culturally safe care. Improve the conditions underneath, like housing, education and income, slower but longer lasting. And give communities control, because programs run with a community get used and kept.
Two things to remember. Read every trend for direction, shape, distribution and cause. And averages are where inequities hide.

Two exam questions. First. A student writes: smoking rates in Australia have gone down. Rewrite this description as an analysis, using direction or shape, distribution, and cause, without quoting any figures. Pause here to answer.

Smoking has fallen steadily for decades, which is direction and shape. But the fall has been slower in lower-income and remote groups, so the gap between groups hasn't closed, which is distribution. That pattern suggests taxes, plain packaging and smoke-free laws worked unevenly, or that norms and stress keep some groups smoking, which is cause. The classic mistake is adding a number instead of a meaning.

scenes.title: attempt two (the average that hid a group)

voiceover.text: Second. A report says deaths from one condition have fallen a lot over twenty years, a public health success. A second table shows the fall is much smaller outside the major cities. Explain what the second table adds, give two possible causes, and say what you'd measure next. Pause here to answer.

The national fall is real, but it's an average. The second table shows a gap widening by place, so the success hasn't reached everyone. Possible causes: less access to specialists and emergency care outside cities, and more risk, like higher smoking. Next, measure the gap by remoteness over time, and travel time to care. The classic mistake is rejecting the national finding instead of qualifying it.

So, for any health data, read the trend in four ways, check whether the average hides a group, and finish with what should be done. Those group rows are where the next questions start. The first is the largest and most persistent gap. What actually improves Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health?
